transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

I’m here because… honestly, I’m exhausted. For about a year now I’ve been trying to get someone to take seriously that parts of my dad’s lab results are being changed, or held back, somewhere in the clinic system. I know how that sounds, but I work around labs, I know what numbers and charts are supposed to look like, and what I saw before does not match what ends up being shown later.

Every time I bring it up, doctors say his numbers are fine, or my family tells me I’m overreacting, or that I misunderstood something, but I didn’t. I know what I saw. The chart doesn’t line up, and it feels like someone is smoothing it over or hiding pieces of it. I’ve been trying to prove it, trying to track who had access and when, and it’s just… it’s taking over everything and wearing me down.
Do you think someone is intentionally changing or hiding your dad's lab results?

Yes. I mean… I don’t know the exact person’s name, and that’s part of what’s driving me crazy, but yes, I think someone in the clinic system is either changing parts of the results or holding things back before the final chart is shown.

It’s not just me being nervous about my dad. I saw numbers and pieces of the chart that did not match what was there later. And every time I try to point that out, people act like I’m confused or like I don’t understand labs, but I do this for work. I know what these things are supposed to look like. Doctors keep saying his numbers are fine, my family keeps telling me to let it go, but I know what I saw. The chart doesn’t line up, and it feels like it’s being smoothed over somehow. I’ve spent so much time trying to figure out who had access, when something changed, where the missing pieces went… and it’s just worn me down completely.
Do you think this situation with your dad's lab results is part of a larger conspiracy or plan?

I don’t know if I’d call it a larger conspiracy exactly… I’m not saying there’s some huge group or something with a plan written down. But I do think someone in the clinic system is doing something, yes. Changing parts of the results, or holding them back, or only letting certain parts show up in the final chart.

Because this has been going on for about a year, and I’ve been trying to prove it the whole time. It’s not just one little number I misread. I work around labs, I know what results are supposed to look like, and what I saw before does not match what everyone keeps showing me later. And every time I bring it up, it’s like the same response: doctors say my dad’s numbers are fine, my family says I’m overreacting, people act like I’m confused. But I know what I saw.

So… bigger plan? I don’t know. But something is being covered up or smoothed over in the clinic system, and it’s worn me down trying to figure out who touched the chart, when it changed, and why nobody will take that seriously.
Do you think this is happening to you and your dad specifically, or could it be happening to other patients as well?

I keep going back and forth on that. At first I thought it was just my dad, because it’s his chart, his results, and I’m the one who saw that things didn’t match later. So that’s the part I can talk about for sure — or as sure as I can be — that something with his labs is being changed or held back somewhere in the clinic system.

But then I think… if someone can do it with his results, why would it only be him? I don’t have proof about other patients, and I’m not trying to accuse the whole place of everything, but it makes me wonder. Because nobody will acknowledge even the obvious mismatch in his chart. The doctors keep saying his numbers are fine, my family keeps telling me I’m overreacting, and it’s like everyone wants me to just stop asking. But I know what I saw before, and it doesn’t line up with what’s showing now.

So I guess my honest answer is: I know it’s happening with my dad’s lab results, and I’m worried it could be happening to others too. But my focus has been on proving what happened with him, because that’s what has taken over my life for the past year.
Do you think you would still be concerned about your dad's lab results if everyone, including doctors and your family, agreed that there was a mistake and it was being investigated?

If they actually agreed there was a mistake and were really investigating it… I think that would help, yes. I mean, that’s what I’ve been asking for this whole time — for somebody to stop brushing me off and say, “Okay, something doesn’t match here, let’s look into it.”

But I don’t think I’d instantly be calm, if that’s what you mean. Because this has been going on for a year. I’ve spent so much time trying to prove that parts of my dad’s lab results were changed or held back somewhere in the clinic system, and every time I brought it up, I was told the numbers were fine, or that I was misunderstanding, or my family would say I needed to let it go. So if suddenly everyone agreed, I’d still want to know what happened, who accessed the chart, what was changed, what was missing, and why nobody took it seriously before.

So yes, I’d probably still be concerned until I saw the investigation actually explain the mismatch. But I wouldn’t feel so alone in it. The worst part has been knowing the chart doesn’t match what I saw and having everyone act like that can’t be true. It’s just worn me down.
Do you think your concerns about your dad's lab results would be considered irrational or unreasonable by most people?

I mean… most people already do think it’s unreasonable, don’t they? That’s been the whole problem. The doctors keep telling me his numbers are fine, my family keeps saying I’m overreacting, like I’ve gotten stuck on something and I should just drop it.

But from where I’m sitting, it doesn’t feel irrational. I know what I saw. I work around labs, I know charts don’t just feel “off” for no reason. The results I remember seeing don’t match what’s being shown now, and I’ve been trying for the past year to prove that someone in the clinic system changed something or held parts back. So if most people call that unreasonable, I guess they’re saying that because they didn’t see what I saw, or because they trust the system more than I do right now.

I can understand that to someone on the outside it might look like I’m fixated on it. I know I’ve spent a lot of time on it, and it’s worn me down. But I don’t think it’s irrational to keep asking questions when my dad’s chart doesn’t match what I saw and everyone just keeps insisting everything is fine.
Has your preoccupation with your dad's lab results been affecting your daily life or relationships in any significant way?

Yes… it has. I don’t really like admitting that, because then it sounds like everyone is right that I’m “too focused” on it, but yes, it’s affected things.

With my family, I can tell they’re starting to work around me. Like with my dad’s appointments, there are plans I find out about later, or they’ll say, “Oh, we already talked to the clinic,” or “We didn’t want to get you upset.” And to me that feels awful, because I’m the one who has been paying attention to the chart and the labs. I’m not trying to make things harder for them, I’m trying to protect him. But I can feel them leaving me out of some of the appointment planning now, and that just makes me more worried because then I don’t know what’s being said or what’s being documented.

And at work… I mean, I’m a phlebotomist, so records and labs are not some abstract thing to me. I know how important accuracy is. But I think people there have started seeing me as someone who gets too intense about record problems. I used to feel like I might be considered for more responsibility, maybe lab supervision at some point, but now I get the sense that’s not happening. Like they think if there’s a chart issue or documentation issue, I’m going to make it confrontational instead of just handling it quietly. Nobody has said it exactly like that, but you can feel when you’re not being looked at the same way anymore.

So yes, it’s affected my relationships and my daily life. I still think the lab issue is real, but I can’t pretend it hasn’t cost me things.
Would you change your mind about your dad's lab results being altered if new evidence came out that contradicted your current beliefs?

I mean… it would depend on what you mean by “evidence.” If it was just another doctor saying, “No, the numbers are fine,” then no, probably not, because I’ve heard that over and over for the past year and it hasn’t explained why the chart doesn’t match what I saw.

If there was actual evidence — like a clear audit trail, something showing who accessed the results, when they were entered, whether anything was corrected or withheld, and it really accounted for the mismatch — then I would try to take that seriously. I’m not trying to believe this for no reason. I’m here because I’ve spent all this time trying to prove that someone in the clinic system changed or held back parts of my dad’s lab results, and it’s exhausting. It’s worn me down. I don’t want to be fighting everybody about it.

But I can’t just change my mind because people tell me I should. That’s the part that makes me sound stubborn, I know. It’s just… I know what I saw, and the chart now doesn’t line up with that. So if new evidence contradicted me, it would have to actually explain that, not just dismiss it. If it did explain it in a way that made sense, maybe I could reconsider. But I’d need to see it for myself.
Do you think your belief about your dad's lab results would change if you were shown the original, unaltered records?

If you showed me what you’re calling the original, unaltered records… I mean, I would look at them, of course. I’m not refusing to look. But I don’t think just handing me a printout and saying, “See, these are original,” would automatically change my mind.

That’s the problem I keep running into. For the past year I’ve been trying to prove that someone in the clinic system changed something or held parts of my dad’s lab results back, and every time I’m told, “No, the numbers are fine,” it doesn’t actually answer the part that bothers me. The chart I remember seeing doesn’t match what’s being shown now. That’s not something I can just erase because someone presents another copy and says it’s unaltered.

I’d need to know where those records came from, who had access, whether there’s an audit trail, whether anything was corrected or hidden before I saw it. Because if the system is the thing I’m worried about, then records from that same system don’t automatically reassure me, if that makes sense.

I know how that sounds. I know it sounds like I’m setting the bar too high, and maybe that’s why people get frustrated with me. But I’m here because this has been wearing me down. I don’t want to keep fighting doctors and my family. I just… I know what I saw, and until something explains why it doesn’t match the chart now, I don’t think my belief would really change.
Do you think your concerns about the lab results would be considered normal by others who have experienced similar situations with their family members?

I think… some of it would be normal, yes. Like, if it’s your parent and you think something is wrong with their medical information, of course you’re going to be concerned. I work around labs, so to me it doesn’t feel strange to pay attention to numbers, dates, what’s in the chart, what got entered, what didn’t. Families question things all the time when they’re worried.

But I also know most people probably wouldn’t still be on it the way I am after this long. That’s where I get stuck. Because for the past year I’ve been trying to prove that someone in the clinic system is changing or holding back parts of my dad’s lab results, and everyone keeps acting like I should just accept that the numbers are fine. Doctors say it, my family says it, and they look at me like I’m making it bigger than it is.

But the chart doesn’t match what I saw. That’s the part I can’t get past. So would other people think it’s normal? Maybe at first, maybe if they understood how serious chart accuracy is. But I think a lot of people would say I’ve gone too far with it, or that I’m wearing myself out over something they don’t see.

And I am worn down. I’ll admit that. It’s exhausting to keep feeling like you’re the only one noticing something important and everyone else just wants you to stop talking about it. So… I don’t know if others would call it normal, but to me it still feels like the concern makes sense because I know what I saw.
Do you think your concerns about your dad's lab results would be considered delusional by a mental health professional?

I guess… yes, I think some mental health professional might call it that. Or at least they might write it down that way because they weren’t there and they didn’t see what I saw. I know how it sounds when I say it out loud — that I believe someone in the clinic system may have changed or held back parts of my dad’s lab results. I know that sounds extreme to people.

But from my side, it doesn’t feel like I just made up an idea and then decided to cling to it. I work around labs, I know charts can be corrected, things can be entered wrong, people can miss things. And I keep coming back to the same point: the chart now does not match what I remember seeing. That’s the part no one really answers. They just say, “The numbers are fine,” or “You need to let this go,” and that makes me feel like they’re skipping over the actual problem.

So if you’re asking would a professional think my concern is not based in reality… maybe. I can admit that. Especially because it’s been a year and I’m still trying to prove it, and it has taken over more of my life than I wanted it to. It’s wearing me down. My family is tired of hearing about it, doctors get impatient, and I’m sitting here still feeling like something happened with those records.

But I don’t think calling it that makes the mismatch disappear. That’s where I get stuck. I can understand that someone might label it that way, but I still know what I saw, and I still don’t feel like anyone has explained why the chart doesn’t line up.
Would seeing the original lab results with a clear explanation of any discrepancies change your belief about what happened to your dad's records?

It would depend on what you mean by “clear explanation,” I guess. I don’t want to sound like I’m saying nothing could ever change my mind, because that’s not how I want to be. If someone sat down with me and actually walked me through the original lab results, where they came from, what changed, why it looked different from what I saw, who entered what, and when… I would listen. I really would.

But if the explanation is just, “These are the real results, you misunderstood,” then no, I don’t think that would change it. Because I’ve been living with this for a year now, trying to prove that someone in the clinic system changed something or held parts of my dad’s lab results back, and it’s not because I enjoy arguing with doctors or upsetting my family. It’s because the chart I remember seeing doesn’t match what’s there now.

That’s the thing everyone keeps skipping over. They keep telling me the numbers are fine, or that I need to let it go, but that doesn’t explain why it was different before. And maybe I’m too focused on it, I can admit that. It’s worn me down. I think about it constantly, and I know people are tired of hearing me bring it up.

So… if there was a truly clear explanation that actually accounted for the discrepancy, maybe it could help. But I’d need it to be more than reassurance. I’d need it to make sense with what I saw. Because right now, I still feel like something happened with those records.
Do you think there is any possible evidence or explanation that could completely change your mind about your dad's lab results being altered?

I want to say yes, because I know that’s probably the reasonable answer. Like, if there were some complete, undeniable explanation, then of course I should be able to change my mind. I don’t want to be someone who can’t take in evidence.

But honestly… I don’t know what would completely change it. That’s the problem. Because I’m here because for the past year I’ve been trying to prove that someone in the clinic system is changing or holding back parts of my dad’s lab results. And no matter how many doctors or family members tell me the numbers are fine, I still come back to the same thing: the chart doesn’t match what I saw.

If someone could show me something that explained that exact mismatch — not just reassure me, not just tell me I’m stressed or misunderstanding it, but actually show me why it looked one way and then later looked different — maybe that would make a difference. I think it would have to be really clear, like step by step, with where the result came from and why the record appears the way it does now.

But “the labs are normal” doesn’t change my mind. My family saying I’m wearing myself down doesn’t change it. Doctors saying there’s nothing wrong doesn’t change it. Because that still doesn’t answer the part that keeps looping in my head.

So… is there possible evidence? Maybe. I’m trying to leave room for that. But completely change my mind? I don’t know. It would have to account for what I saw, because I know what I saw, and I can’t just pretend I don’t.
Do you think it's possible that your perception of the lab results being altered is not based in reality?

I mean… I can say the words “maybe it’s possible,” because I know sitting here with you, that’s probably what you’re asking me to consider. And I’m not trying to be impossible or act like I’m the only person who can ever be right.

But it doesn’t feel that way to me. It doesn’t feel like this is just some mistaken perception I had and then built a whole story around. I’m here because for the past year I’ve been trying to prove that someone in the clinic system is changing or holding back parts of my dad’s lab results, and no matter how many doctors or my family tell me the numbers are fine, I keep coming back to the same thing: the chart doesn’t match what I saw.

And that’s what wears me down, honestly. Because if I could just believe I misread it, or I got confused, maybe I could stop. I want to stop thinking about it so much. I’m tired. But every time I try to let it go, it’s like my mind goes right back to that mismatch. It feels real because I remember seeing it differently.

So… is it possible, in some outside way, that I’m wrong? I guess I have to admit it’s possible. But inside, no, I don’t really believe that. I still feel like something happened with those records, and nobody has explained it in a way that actually makes sense to me.
Do you think there is anything that could happen or anything someone could show you that would make you completely give up your belief that your dad's lab results were altered?

I don’t know. I mean, I know I’ve kind of answered this already, but that’s honestly where I get stuck. Part of me wants to say, “Yes, if someone showed me the original records and explained everything, I’d let it go,” because that sounds reasonable. And I want to be reasonable. I’m not trying to spend my life chasing this.

But completely give it up? That’s harder. Because I’m here because for the past year I’ve been trying to prove that someone in the clinic system changed something or held back parts of my dad’s lab results. And everyone keeps focusing on the wrong part, at least that’s how it feels to me. They say, “The numbers are fine,” or “The doctors said there’s nothing wrong,” or my family says I’m wearing myself down, which… I am. I know I am. But that still doesn’t answer why the chart I remember seeing doesn’t match what’s there now.

So if someone could show me something that accounted for that exact thing — not just a printout, not just reassurance, but something that showed why it looked different to me before and why it looks the way it does now — maybe that would help. Maybe it would loosen it. But I don’t know if it would make me completely give it up, because I know what I saw. That’s the part I can’t get past.

I wish I could say there’s one thing that would settle it, because I’m tired of thinking about it all the time. It’s wearing me down. But right now, no one has shown me anything that makes the mismatch make sense. So I guess my honest answer is… maybe in theory, but I can’t really picture what would make me fully stop believing something happened with those records.
Would your belief about your dad's lab results change if an independent investigation found no evidence of tampering?

If an independent investigation said they found no evidence of tampering… I mean, I’d want to know exactly what they looked at. That’s where my mind goes right away. Who did the investigation, what records did they have access to, did they look at the original entries, the timestamps, who opened the chart, whether anything was corrected or removed… because just saying “no evidence” doesn’t automatically settle it for me.

I know that probably sounds like I’m moving the goalposts, and maybe that’s what people think I’m doing. But I’m here because for the past year I’ve been trying to prove that someone in the clinic system is changing or holding back parts of my dad’s lab results, and everyone keeps telling me the numbers are fine. Doctors, my family, everybody. And I hear them, but I still know the chart doesn’t match what I saw. That’s the part that keeps me stuck.

So would it change my belief? Maybe it would make me pause. Maybe if it was truly independent and they explained it in a way that matched the exact thing I remember seeing, it might take some of the pressure off. But if it was just a report saying, “We found no evidence,” I don’t think that would completely change my mind. I’d still be thinking, okay, but did they look in the right place? Did they miss what happened? Was it already covered up by then?

I don’t want to keep living like this. It’s wearing me down. I know it is. But I can’t just accept a conclusion that doesn’t explain the mismatch. That’s the problem. It’s not enough for someone to tell me everything is fine if the chart still doesn’t make sense compared to what I saw.
Do you think there is anything that could convince you that your dad's lab results were not altered, no matter how small the chance?

I mean… no matter how small the chance? That’s hard, because I know the answer I’m probably supposed to give is, “Yes, of course, evidence could convince me.” And part of me wants to say that, because I don’t want you to think I’m completely closed off or that I’m just refusing to hear anything.

But if I’m being honest, I don’t know what would fully convince me. That’s the problem. I keep coming back to the same thing over and over: I’m here because for the past year I’ve been trying to prove that someone in the clinic system changed something or held back part of my dad’s lab results. And no matter how many doctors tell me the numbers are fine, or how many times my family says I’m misunderstanding it or wearing myself down, I still know the chart doesn’t match what I saw.

It’s not even just about wanting someone to say, “The labs are normal.” I’ve heard that. I’ve heard it so many times. But that doesn’t answer the part that keeps bothering me. It’s the mismatch. It’s that I remember seeing something different, and then later it wasn’t there the same way. So when someone says nothing was altered, my mind immediately goes, okay, but then why doesn’t it match? Why do I remember it so clearly?

So… maybe there is something, in theory, that could convince me. Like if someone could explain every single part of it in a way that actually fit what I saw, not just dismiss it. But right now I can’t really picture it. Even if the chance is small, I’d still feel like there’s something that happened with those records. And I know that sounds exhausting, because it is. It’s wearing me down. I want there to be an answer that lets me stop thinking about it, but I don’t have one that makes me feel sure the results weren’t altered.
Would you accept an external review of your dad's lab results by an independent medical expert as conclusive evidence to resolve your concerns?

I would consider it, yes… I mean, I’m not against an outside expert looking at it. In some ways that’s what I’ve been asking for, because I don’t feel like anyone inside the clinic system is going to really look at what happened with the chart. But “conclusive” is where I get stuck.

If it was an independent medical expert, I’d want to know what they actually reviewed. Did they just look at the lab numbers as they exist now and say, “These are fine”? Because that wouldn’t resolve it for me. That’s what people keep doing — doctors, my family, everyone — they keep telling me the numbers are fine, and I understand that’s supposed to reassure me, but it doesn’t answer the part I keep coming back to. The chart doesn’t match what I saw.

I’ve been trying for the past year to prove that someone in the clinic system changed something or held back part of my dad’s lab results, and it’s not because I want there to be some big problem. I don’t. I’m tired. It’s wearing me down, honestly. But if the external review didn’t explain that mismatch, then I don’t think I could accept it as the final word.

So… I’d accept the review being done. I’d read it. I’d try to take it seriously. But as conclusive evidence? Only if it actually addressed the specific thing I’m talking about — why I remember seeing one thing and why the chart looks different now. If it just says everything is normal, then no, I don’t think that would be enough for me to let it go.
Do you think your belief about your dad's lab results is based on reality?

Yes. I do. I know that’s probably not the answer you’re looking for, or maybe it sounds like I’m too certain, but from my side it feels based on something real because I saw what I saw. I’m not making it up to cause trouble, and I’m not trying to be difficult with the doctors or my family.

For the past year I’ve been trying to prove that someone in the clinic system changed something or held back parts of my dad’s lab results. And every time someone tells me, “The numbers are fine,” I understand what they’re saying, but it doesn’t answer the actual problem for me. The chart now doesn’t match what I remember seeing. That’s the part I can’t get past.

So when you ask if it’s based on reality, I guess I’d say yes, because to me the mismatch is real. The fact that everyone else keeps saying there’s nothing wrong doesn’t erase that. It makes me feel more cornered, honestly, because I’m trying to explain something that feels obvious to me, and people keep treating it like I’m just confused.

I don’t want this to be my life. It’s wearing me down. But I can’t honestly sit here and say, “No, it isn’t real,” when I still know the chart doesn’t match what I saw.

I would consider it, yes… I mean, I’m not against an outside expert looking at it. In some ways that’s what I’ve been asking for, because I don’t feel like anyone inside the clinic system is going to really look at what happened with the chart. But “conclusive” is where I get stuck.

If it was an independent medical expert, I’d want to know what they actually reviewed. Did they just look at the lab numbers as they exist now and say, “These are fine”? Because that wouldn’t resolve it for me. That’s what people keep doing — doctors, my family, everyone — they keep telling me the numbers are fine, and I understand that’s supposed to reassure me, but it doesn’t answer the part I keep coming back to. The chart doesn’t match what I saw.

I’ve been trying for the past year to prove that someone in the clinic system changed something or held back part of my dad’s lab results, and it’s not because I want there to be some big problem. I don’t. I’m tired. It’s wearing me down, honestly. But if the external review didn’t explain that mismatch, then I don’t think I could accept it as the final word.

So… I’d accept the review being done. I’d read it. I’d try to take it seriously. But as conclusive evidence? Only if it actually addressed the specific thing I’m talking about — why I remember seeing one thing and why the chart looks different now. If it just says everything is normal, then no, I don’t think that would be enough for me to let it go.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of delusional thinking
doctor.question: Do you think your belief about your dad's lab results is based on reality?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I’m here because for the past year I’ve been trying to prove that someone in the clinic system is changing or holding back parts of my dad’s lab results, and no matter how many doctors or family members tell me the numbers are fine, I know the chart doesn’t match what I saw and it’s wearing me down.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking whether the patient recognizes the belief about the lab results as reality-based, which assesses the fixed delusional belief.

patient.answer:
Yes. I do. I know that’s probably not the answer you’re looking for, or maybe it sounds like I’m too certain, but from my side it feels based on something real because I saw what I saw. I’m not making it up to cause trouble, and I’m not trying to be difficult with the doctors or my family.

For the past year I’ve been trying to prove that someone in the clinic system changed something or held back parts of my dad’s lab results. And every time someone tells me, “The numbers are fine,” I understand what they’re saying, but it doesn’t answer the actual problem for me. The chart now doesn’t match what I remember seeing. That’s the part I can’t get past.

So when you ask if it’s based on reality, I guess I’d say yes, because to me the mismatch is real. The fact that everyone else keeps saying there’s nothing wrong doesn’t erase that. It makes me feel more cornered, honestly, because I’m trying to explain something that feels obvious to me, and people keep treating it like I’m just confused.

I don’t want this to be my life. It’s wearing me down. But I can’t honestly sit here and say, “No, it isn’t real,” when I still know the chart doesn’t match what I saw.

inference.note: F41.0 was ruled out as the patient's beliefs, although persistent, are focused on a specific, verifiable issue (the lab results) rather than a broader, unfounded fear or anxiety pattern typical of anxiety disorders. F32.0 remains as the patient's emotional state and behavior could also suggest a depressive episode, given the significant impact on daily life and relationships. F22 remains a strong candidate as the patient's belief about the lab results being altered, despite contrary evidence and reassurance, aligns with delusional disorder.
